newsitem.title: USA: Chicago Fed challenges Midwest trade/weak dlr link.
newsitem.headline: Chicago Fed challenges Midwest trade/weak dlr link.

text.p: U.S. manufacturing exports from the Midwest grew at a rapid pace over the past decade despite a stronger -- not a weaker -- dollar, according to economists at the Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago.

"The conventional wisdom was...that the sharp depreciation of the dollar during the period 1985-1987, and a gradual depreciation of the dollar since then, materially contributed to Midwest manufacturing industries' ability to compete in export markets," Chicago Fed economists Jack Hervey and William Strauss said in a research paper.

"The common perception is that the dollar has recorded a secular depreciation during the past 25 years. But has it really?" Hervey and Strauss questioned in the paper they presented at a day-long conference on "Global Linkages to the Midwest Economy" held at the Chicago Fed on Wednesday.
The conference is part of a year-long Chicago Fed research project on the Midwest economy.

Hervey and Strauss noted that, since the United States abandoned the gold standard in 1971, the dollar has declined against some currencies, appreciated against others or remained stable against a third group.

The Chicago Fed economists argued that, to better assess the export/dollar relationship, it would be useful to look at the dollar's performance versus a specific basket of currencies representing the main export markets of any given U.S. region.

"The premise underlying construction of a regional dollar index maintains that there are differences in the foreign markets, or export shares, served by different geographical regions of the United States," Hervey and Strauss said.
The economists noted that about 43 percent of the Midwest's exports of manufactured goods go to Canada, 13 percent to Mexico, 13 percent to Europe and five percent to Japan.
Nationwide, 23 percent of U.S. exports of manufactured goods go to Canada, 17 percent to Europe, and about 10 percent to Mexico and Japan.

"The export data strongly suggest that Midwest exporters of manufactured goods depend substantially more heavily on foreign markets in which the dollar has actually appreciated in recent years -- Canada and Mexico -- relative to U.S. exporters of manufactured goods overall," Hervey and Strauss noted.
In their study, the economists chose aggregate exchange rates adjusted for inflation differentials between the United States and 44 countries importing U.S. goods.

"Contrary to the common perception, the real dollar did not continue a depreciating trend following the large gyrations recorded during the 1980-1987 period, at least for the Midwest," Hervey and Strauss found. "The aggregate Midwest export-weighted real dollar index shows an appreciating trend for the entire period 1974-1996."
Meanwhile, the annual dollar value of manufactured goods exported from the Midwest rose more than fivefold between 1969 and 1991, Hervey and Strauss estimate.
The Chicago Fed economists concluded the increased competitiveness of U.S. manufacturers was achieved despite the dollar's appreciation in their main export markets.

"Given the foreign markets Midwest manufacturing is active in, it would appear that this increased competitiveness has been accomplished without the help of a depreciating dollar exchange rate, as conventional wisdom has often contended," Hervey and Strauss said.
